topic: Evaluate a redesigned ecommerce checkout flow.
persona: A busy parent who shops online weekly and abandons carts when checkout feels slow or confusing.

transcript.content:
Let's get started with the interview. I'll be taking notes and asking follow-up questions based on your responses.

Can you walk me through your typical online shopping experience, and how often do you shop online for yourself and for your family?

I shop online at least once a week, usually more often when school's in session and I need to restock on household essentials and my kids' supplies. I try to do most of my shopping during naptime or after they're in bed, but sometimes I have to sneak in a quick order during breakfast or lunch when I have a spare minute. I shop for myself maybe once a month, but mostly it's for my family - groceries, diapers, clothes, toys... you name it.

It sounds like you have a pretty busy schedule. 

How do you usually find out about the products or stores you're shopping from - do you get recommendations from friends, see ads online, or use a specific search engine or app?

Honestly, it's usually a mix of things. My friends and family will sometimes send me links to products they think I'd like, or I'll see ads on Facebook or Instagram that catch my eye. I also use a search engine like Google to find specific products or stores, and I've got a few favorite apps like RetailMeNot and Coupons.com that help me save money. But if I'm being completely honest, I often just end up searching for "buy [product name]" or "where to buy [product name]" because I need it ASAP and don't have time to browse around.

It sounds like you're a pretty savvy online shopper.

When you're searching for a product, what factors do you consider most important when deciding whether to make a purchase from a particular website - for example, price, shipping speed, product reviews, or something else?

Price is a big one, no question. If I can find the same product cheaper elsewhere, I'll usually go with the cheaper option. But shipping speed is also really important - if I can get it delivered quickly, that's a big plus. And I'm also a big fan of free shipping, of course! Product reviews can be helpful, but I've learned to take them with a grain of salt - I've seen some fake reviews out there. And if I'm shopping on a mobile device, a smooth checkout process is huge - if it's too slow or confusing, I'll abandon my cart and try a different site.

It sounds like you're looking for a balance between price, convenience, and reliability.

Have you ever experienced a situation where you started to check out on a website, but then abandoned your cart because the checkout process was too slow or confusing - and if so, what specifically made you decide to leave the site?

Yeah, that happens all the time. I think it's happened to me at least half the time I've tried to check out online. Usually it's because I'm asked to create an account or log in, and I just don't have time for that. Or maybe the site is slow to load or doesn't respond quickly enough, so I get impatient and just give up. Sometimes it's because the payment options are too complicated or they're trying to upsell me on something I don't need. But the thing that really gets me is when I have to click through multiple screens to get to the payment page - that's just too many steps for me.

It sounds like you value simplicity and efficiency in the checkout process.

Have you ever noticed any websites that have a particularly streamlined or user-friendly checkout process - one that makes you feel like it's easy to complete your purchase and get on with your day?

Yeah, I have. Amazon's checkout process is actually really seamless. They've got it down to just a few clicks, and it's really easy to save my payment info and shipping addresses so I don't have to re-enter them every time. And they've got those little "one-click" buttons that make it so easy to just click and go. I've also used Walmart's checkout process a few times, and it's pretty smooth too. They've got a mobile app that lets me scan my items and checkout really quickly, which is a lifesaver when I'm trying to get in and out of the house fast.

It sounds like Amazon and Walmart have done a good job of simplifying the checkout process for you.

Have you ever tried to use a mobile app to complete a purchase, and if so, what features do you think make an app checkout process more convenient for you than a traditional website checkout?

Yeah, I use the Target Cartwheel app all the time. It's got a really easy checkout process, and I can just scan my items and pay quickly. I also like that I can save my payment info and shipping addresses right in the app, so I don't have to re-enter them every time. And sometimes they'll even offer me a coupon or discount at checkout, which is a nice bonus. I think what makes app checkout more convenient is that it's just so easy to scan my items and pay right from my phone - it's faster than typing everything in on a computer, and it's just more convenient overall. And some apps will even let me save my cart for later, which is great if I'm not ready to checkout right away.

topic: Evaluate a redesigned ecommerce checkout flow.
persona: A busy parent who shops online weekly and abandons carts when checkout feels slow or confusing.

transcript.content: Can you walk me through your typical online shopping experience, from browsing products to completing a purchase, and tell me about any challenges you've faced during this process?

My typical online shopping experience is pretty straightforward. I usually browse products during naptime or while waiting for my kid's extracurricular activities to finish. When I find something I like, I add it to my cart and proceed to checkout. The problems usually start when it takes too long to enter my payment info or when the site asks for a million different forms of verification. It's frustrating because I've already got all my login info saved, but somehow it still takes an eternity to get through the process.
Have you ever had an experience where you started the checkout process, but then abandoned your cart before completing the purchase due to frustration or feeling like it was taking too long?

Yeah, it happens more often than I'd like to admit. I was trying to order some household essentials last week, and the checkout process kept freezing on me. I had to reload the page multiple times, and by the time I finally got through, I'd forgotten what I was even buying. So, I just bailed on the whole thing and went to a different site that's known for having a smoother checkout process. It's not ideal, but sometimes it's just easier to cut my losses and try again another day.
Can you think of any specific moments or decisions that led you to choose the alternative site with a smoother checkout process, rather than trying to complete the purchase on the original site?

I think what really tipped the scales was when I had to re-enter my entire address, including the apartment number, which I'd already saved on the site. It felt like a total hassle, and I was like, "You know what, I've got better things to do." When I went to the other site, I was able to just log in and have it auto-populate my address. It was a small thing, but it made a big difference for me in that moment.
Are there any specific features or functionalities that you've seen on other ecommerce sites that you wish were available on the site you were trying to use, but weren't?

One thing that really gets me is when a site doesn't have a guest checkout option, but then still asks for a ton of personal info. I'm not always in the mood to create an account, especially if I'm just making a one-time purchase. If the other site had let me check out as a guest, I probably would've stayed on that site. It's just one less hurdle to jump over, you know?

Have you ever tried to create an account on a site, but then found that the process of creating an account was more complicated or time-consuming than you anticipated, and it ultimately led you to abandon your cart?

Yeah, it's happened to me. I was trying to buy some toys for my kid's birthday, and the site asked me to create an account. I thought, "Okay, no big deal, I'll just make an account." But then they asked for like 10 different pieces of info, including a password, email, phone number, and all this other stuff. It was just so much to take in, and I was like, "Wait, do I really need to do all this?" By the time I finally got through it, I'd forgotten what I was buying in the first place.
Did you ever end up using the account you created on that site, or did you abandon it after the initial purchase?

Honestly, I never ended up using the account I created. I just made a purchase and then never went back to the site again. It was one of those things where I just didn't feel like investing the time in setting up an account, and since it was just a one-time purchase, I didn't see the point in creating an account just for that.

transcript.content: Can you walk me through your typical process when checking out on an ecommerce website?

Honestly, I tend to scan the checkout page quickly. I usually look for any promotions or discounts I might have missed earlier in the shopping process, then I check my cart to make sure everything is correct. If I see any issues, I'll pause and fix them before proceeding.
What information do you usually check on the checkout page before proceeding with your order?

I usually check the subtotal, shipping costs, and any additional fees. If I see any unexpected charges, I might pause and try to figure out where they came from. I also double-check my shipping address and payment method to make sure everything is correct.
How do you typically handle unexpected charges or fees that you didn't anticipate when checking out?

If I see unexpected charges or fees, I'll usually pause and try to figure out where they came from. If I'm not sure, I might try to contact customer support or go back to the product page to see if I missed any details. If it's still unclear, I might just abandon the cart and look for a better option elsewhere.
What factors influence your decision to contact customer support or to abandon the cart when you're unsure about charges or fees?

It usually depends on how busy I am. If I'm short on time, I'll just abandon the cart and move on to another website. I'm also more likely to contact support if I've used the website before and had a good experience.
How do you usually perceive the time it takes to resolve an issue with customer support when you're checking out?

To be honest, any delay in resolving an issue feels like an eternity when I'm in a hurry to complete my order. Even if it's just a few minutes, it can feel like a long time when I'm trying to get everything done for the week. If I have to wait on hold or wait for a response, I'm likely to just give up and look for a different website.
What do you think would make you more likely to wait for customer support to resolve an issue while you're checking out?

If the website could give me a clear estimate of how long it would take to resolve the issue, that would be helpful. Or if they had a live chat option that allowed me to communicate with a rep in real-time, that would be better than waiting on hold. I'd also appreciate it if they could offer a temporary hold or a way to save my cart and come back to it later, so I could come back to it when I have more time.

topic: Understand reactions to a student budgeting app that categorizes spending automatically.
persona: A college student with part-time income, inconsistent savings, and mild anxiety about money.

transcript.content:
Let's get started with the interview. I'm here to understand your thoughts and feelings about a new student budgeting app that can automatically categorize your spending. 

Here's my first question:

Have you ever used a budgeting or expense-tracking app before?

I've tried a few, like Mint and Personal Capital, but I never stuck with them for too long. I think I got frustrated with how long it took to set everything up and then I'd forget to update it. It was just too much work, you know? I'd rather just spend my time on actual school stuff.

It can be overwhelming to set up and maintain a budgeting app.

Can you tell me more about what you mean by "actual school stuff" - is that referring to coursework, extracurricular activities, or something else?

It's more like, I'd rather be studying or working on projects for my classes than worrying about how much I spent on coffee or takeout last week. I'm trying to get good grades, and I don't want to stress about money too much, so I kind of put off using these apps. Plus, with school and a part-time job, it feels like I'm already juggling a lot, you know?

It sounds like you have a lot on your plate.

How do you currently keep track of your expenses, if you don't use a budgeting app?

Honestly, I just try to keep track of my spending in my head or in a little notebook. I write down when I pay for things, like bills or groceries, but I don't really keep track of smaller purchases, like coffee or snacks. It's not the most reliable system, but it's what I've been doing so far.

It can be challenging to keep track of all your expenses, especially the smaller ones.

Do you think there's anything that would make it more appealing to you to use a budgeting app, like this one that automatically categorizes your spending?

I think if it was super easy to use and didn't require a lot of setup, that would be a big plus. I'd also want to know that it's secure and not going to sell my info or anything. And maybe if it could give me some kind of alerts or reminders when I'm getting close to going over budget in a certain category... that would be helpful. But I'm not sure if any of those things would be enough to get me to actually use it.

It sounds like you're looking for a pretty seamless experience.

How important is it to you that the app provides personalized advice or recommendations for improving your spending habits, versus just tracking your expenses?

I think it's kind of nice to have some guidance, but at the same time, I don't want to feel judged or lectured about my spending habits. I mean, I know I spend too much on takeout, but I'm trying to cut back, okay? If the app just gives me some general tips or suggestions, that might be okay, but if it's like, "You're wasting so much money on coffee, you need to cut back more," that might just make me feel guilty and not want to use the app.

It sounds like you're looking for a more supportive approach.

Would you be more likely to use a budgeting app if you could customize the way it provides feedback or advice, so it's more tailored to your own goals and preferences?

Yeah, that would be really helpful. If I could set my own goals and priorities, like, "I want to save up for a laptop" or "I want to cut back on dining out," and the app could give me feedback based on that, that would be really useful. And maybe even let me decide how often I get those reminders or suggestions, so it's not overwhelming. That way, I could use the app in a way that feels more personal and not just like some generic, one-size-fits-all thing.

topic: Understand reactions to a student budgeting app that categorizes spending automatically.
persona: A college student with part-time income, inconsistent savings, and mild anxiety about money.

transcript.content: Can you tell me about a time when you had to manually categorize your expenses, such as splitting a bill with friends or tracking your spending for a specific goal?

Ugh, yeah... I remember when I was trying to save up for a concert ticket last semester. I had to manually track my expenses in a spreadsheet to see where I could cut back. It was super tedious, and I kept forgetting to update it, so I'd have to go back and try to remember what I spent money on. I think I ended up using a mix of receipts and old bank statements to figure it out.
What was the most frustrating part about trying to manually track your expenses in that situation?

The worst part was trying to remember what I spent money on. I'd go back to my spreadsheet and be like, "Wait, did I get coffee from Starbucks or from that new coffee shop downtown?" And then I'd have to dig through my receipts or emails to figure it out. It was so time-consuming and stressful, especially when I was trying to meet a deadline to save up for the concert.
Have you ever found yourself avoiding checking your finances or tracking your spending because it felt overwhelming or stressful, and if so, what usually triggered that feeling?

Yeah, that's happened a lot. I'd be trying to avoid opening my bank app or checking my account balance because I'd be worried about how much money I had left or if I'd overspent. It usually triggered when I saw a low balance or when I was about to make a big purchase. It was like, I knew I should be checking my finances regularly, but the anxiety would get the best of me and I'd just put it off.
When you did eventually check your finances, what was going through your mind, and how did you typically respond to what you saw?

When I finally checked my finances, I'd usually feel a mix of guilt and panic. I'd be like, "Oh no, I spent way too much on coffee this week" or "I'm so behind on my savings." It was hard to stay calm and just assess the situation objectively. I'd often respond by trying to cut back on unnecessary expenses or making a plan to pay off my debt, but sometimes I'd just feel overwhelmed and procrastinate on actually making changes.

Do you think that having an automatic categorization system in a budgeting app would have made a difference in how you managed your finances during that time when you were trying to save up for the concert ticket?

I think it would've been a game-changer. Having an app that could automatically categorize my expenses would've saved me so much time and stress. I wouldn't have had to spend hours digging through receipts and trying to remember what I spent money on. It would've given me a clear picture of where my money was going, and I could've made more informed decisions about where to cut back. It might've even helped me stick to my budget and reach my savings goal faster.

If you had access to an automatic categorization system in a budgeting app, do you think you would use it regularly to monitor your spending and stay on top of your finances, or would you likely only use it when you're trying to meet a specific savings goal?

Honestly, I think I'd probably only use it when I'm trying to meet a specific goal, like saving up for a big purchase or paying off debt. I'm not sure I'd make it a habit to regularly check my spending and balance, even with the automatic categorization system. I'd probably just check in when I'm feeling anxious or stressed about my finances, and then go back to ignoring it.

I've tried using a budgeting app before, but I gave up on it after a few weeks because it was too complicated.

I'd also like to see some kind of visual representation of my spending, like a pie chart or something, to help me see where my money is going. And maybe some kind of reminder or alert system to help me stay on track with my expenses.
How do you think you would use a visual representation of your spending, such as a pie chart, to inform your financial decisions?

I think it would help me see at a glance where I'm spending most of my money. Like, if I see that I'm spending way more on dining out than I am on groceries, I might think twice about ordering takeout for lunch. Or, if I see that my entertainment budget is really high, I might try to plan some free events or activities for the month instead of spending money on concerts or movies. It's not that I wouldn't know I'm overspending – it's just that sometimes it's hard to make changes when you're not really seeing the numbers in front of you.
What role do you think emotions, such as anxiety or guilt, play in your spending decisions?

Definitely a big role. I feel guilty when I spend money on things that I don't really need, like buying a bunch of clothes at the beginning of the semester when I know I'll just end up wearing them a few times. It's like, I know I shouldn't be spending that money, but at the same time, it's hard to resist the urge to treat myself. And when I'm feeling anxious about money, I tend to make more impulsive purchases – like buying a coffee or a snack when I'm stressed – just to try and take my mind off things. It's not really a rational decision, but it's just what I do.
Can you describe a situation where you made an impulsive purchase due to financial anxiety, and how you felt afterwards?

Yeah... I was feeling really overwhelmed with school and work and stuff, and I was stressing about how I was going to pay my bills on time. I was walking home from campus and I saw this really cute pair of shoes at a store, and I just felt this overwhelming urge to buy them. I know it was a stupid thing to do, but it felt like I was treating myself, like I deserved it after all the stress I'd been dealing with. But as soon as I got home and saw the price tag, I was like, "Wait, why did I just spend $100 on shoes?" It was this huge weight on my shoulders, and I felt guilty and anxious all over again. It was like, I'd just made things worse instead of better.
How do you think you might use a budgeting app to help you manage your financial anxiety, if you were to use one regularly?

I think seeing my spending in black and white, like with the automatic categorization feature, would really help me get a handle on things. It's hard to ignore the numbers when they're staring me in the face. I'd also like to see some kind of stress-tracking feature, where I can log how I'm feeling and see if there's a correlation between my anxiety and my spending. Maybe it could even send me reminders or suggestions for ways to manage my stress, like exercise or meditation. That way, I could try to address the root of the problem instead of just treating the symptoms with impulsive purchases.

topic: Get feedback on a telehealth appointment booking experience.
persona: A working adult who books medical appointments for themselves and an elderly parent.

transcript.content:
Let's get started with the interview. 

Can you walk me through your typical process for booking a telehealth appointment for yourself or your elderly parent, and what motivated you to choose telehealth in the first place?

So, for me, I usually book telehealth appointments when I'm short on time or can't make it to the doctor's office. I've used it a few times for myself, like when I had a minor cold and didn't want to take the whole day off work. I'd say about 80% of the time, it's for my mom, though. She's elderly and has mobility issues, so it's just easier for her to stay at home. We usually book appointments with her primary care physician or a specialist she sees regularly for her chronic conditions.

To book an appointment, I usually log in to the doctor's portal or use their app. Sometimes I have to call the office to get the login info or to book the appointment over the phone. I've had some issues with the app crashing or not loading correctly, but overall, it's worked out okay. I do wish it were easier to see the appointment availability and prices upfront before I book, but that's about it.

You mentioned using the doctor's portal or app to book appointments. Have you ever used a third-party platform or website to book a telehealth appointment, such as a telemedicine marketplace or a patient engagement platform?

Yeah, I've used a few third-party platforms to book telehealth appointments for my mom. I think it was a patient engagement platform that our insurance company recommended. They had a list of participating doctors and specialties, and I could filter by location, availability, and even price. It was pretty convenient, but I did have to create an account with them, which was a bit of a hassle. I also had to deal with some issues when trying to access my mom's records through their platform, which was a bit of a pain. I'm not sure if it was worth the extra steps, to be honest.

It sounds like the third-party platform offered some benefits, but also some challenges. Did you find that the experience of booking a telehealth appointment through the platform differed significantly from booking directly through your mom's doctor's office?

Yeah, it was definitely different. With the platform, I felt like I had more control over the process, being able to compare prices and availability. But at the same time, it felt a bit impersonal, like I was just booking a generic appointment rather than working with my mom's actual doctor. And sometimes the platform would send automated reminders or follow-up emails, which was nice, but also felt a bit pushy. Booking directly through the doctor's office, on the other hand, felt more like I was working with people I knew and trusted. It's hard to put my finger on it, but the platform just felt a bit more transactional, you know?

That's an interesting contrast. How do you think the experience of booking a telehealth appointment through the platform would change if the platform was integrated more closely with your mom's doctor's office, so that you could still get the benefits of comparison and convenience, but also felt like you were still working with her doctor and their office?

If the platform was integrated more closely with the doctor's office, I think that would make a big difference. I'd feel more confident that I was still working with the same people and systems that I trust. And it would be nice to have the convenience of comparison shopping and booking online, but still have that personal touch. I'd imagine it would be like booking an appointment directly through the office, but with the added benefits of the platform.

One thing that might be nice is if the platform could somehow show me information about my mom's history and previous appointments with her doctor, so I could see the context of what's going on. And maybe even some personalized recommendations for doctors or appointment times based on her needs. But yeah, if it felt like I was still working with her doctor's office, I think I'd be more likely to use the platform.

That's a great idea about showing information about your mom's history and previous appointments. Have you ever had to provide this kind of information to the doctor or their staff when booking a telehealth appointment, and if so, how did that experience go for you?

Yeah, I've had to provide some of that information before, and it can be a bit of a pain. Usually, I have to log in to the doctor's portal or call the office to get the info, and then I have to relay it to the person booking the appointment. It's not always easy to get everything transferred over, and sometimes I worry that something gets lost in translation. Like, I'll remind them to mention my mom's medication list or her recent test results, but I'm not always sure if they actually take note of it.

It would be really helpful if the platform could somehow sync with the doctor's office and automatically pull up that information, so I wouldn't have to repeat it every time. Or at least if there was a way to upload documents or share info directly with the doctor, that would be a big time-saver. As it is, it's just a lot of phone calls and back-and-forth, which can be frustrating.

It sounds like having a more seamless way to share information would be really helpful. Have you ever considered using a personal health record (PHR) or a patient portal that allows you to store and manage your mom's medical information in one place, and then share it with her healthcare providers as needed?

Yeah, I've thought about that. Actually, my mom's primary care physician's office has a PHR system that they use, and it's been really helpful for sharing information between our providers. But it's not always easy to use, to be honest. The interface can be a bit clunky, and sometimes I have to dig through a lot of menus to find the info I'm looking for.

I've also tried using some of the more consumer-facing PHR platforms, like MyChart or Microsoft HealthVault, but they've been a bit of a mixed bag. Some of them have been really easy to use and have a lot of features, but others have been more complicated or just not very user-friendly. And sometimes I worry about the security of sharing sensitive medical info online.

But yeah, I can see how a good PHR system could be really helpful for managing my mom's care and sharing info with her providers. If it were more streamlined and user-friendly, I'd definitely consider using it more.

topic: Get feedback on a telehealth appointment booking experience.
persona: A working adult who books medical appointments for themselves and an elderly parent.

transcript.content: Can you walk me through your most recent experience booking a telehealth appointment for yourself or your elderly parent - what specifically led you to choose a telehealth option over an in-person visit?

My mom had a scheduled appointment with her cardiologist, and she was experiencing some chest pain. I knew it was better for her to see the doctor sooner rather than later, but traffic in our area can be really bad, and I didn't want her to risk getting delayed or worse. So, I opted for a telehealth appointment. I chose it because it allowed her to see the doctor from the comfort of her home, and I could even stay with her to help if needed, which was a big plus. Plus, it was a weekday evening, and I was worried about finding parking near the hospital.
How did you find the process of preparing for the telehealth appointment - was there anything in particular that made it easy or difficult to get set up and ready to go?

The preparation process was pretty straightforward, but I did have to troubleshoot a few issues to get everything working. The doctor's office sent us a link to download the telehealth platform, but the link didn't work on my mom's tablet, so I had to switch to my laptop, which was a bit of a hassle. They also required us to create an account and fill out some paperwork beforehand, which took some time, but I guess it's necessary for their records. Once we got everything set up, it was smooth sailing.

Looking back, are there any steps in the preparation process that you think could be simplified or made easier, even if it's just a minor adjustment, that might make the experience feel less frustrating or time-consuming?

Yeah, definitely. One thing that would be helpful is if they could provide a more detailed guide on how to troubleshoot common issues, like what to do if the link doesn't work or if the internet connection is weak. It would save me time and frustration trying to figure things out on my own. Also, maybe they could allow us to save the link or the account info somewhere, like a secure note, so we don't have to dig it up every time. Little things like that can make a big difference.

Have you ever had to cancel or reschedule a telehealth appointment, and if so, what was that experience like - was it similar to canceling or rescheduling an in-person appointment, or were there any differences you noticed?

Yeah, we had to reschedule my mom's appointment at the last minute because the cardiologist had an unexpected emergency. The process was similar to canceling an in-person appointment, but it was a bit more confusing because we had to use the telehealth platform to notify the doctor's office. I had to log in and fill out a form to reschedule, which was a bit of a hassle. I wish it was more streamlined, like being able to call or text the office directly, but I guess that's just the nature of digital communication.

When you had to reschedule the appointment, did you have any issues with communication with the doctor's office or the telehealth platform - for example, did you receive timely reminders or updates about the new appointment time, or were there any misunderstandings that needed to be cleared up?

The communication was a bit spotty. We didn't receive any reminders about the new appointment time, and I had to follow up with the doctor's office to confirm it. I also tried to log in to the telehealth platform to check the new appointment time, but it still showed the original date and time. It wasn't a huge issue, but it was a bit frustrating to have to keep chasing down updates. I think they could do a better job of keeping patients informed and up-to-date on any changes.

Are there any features or functionalities that you think would be useful to have in a telehealth appointment booking system that you haven't seen or experienced yet, but think would make a big difference in your overall experience?

One thing that would be really helpful is if the system could automatically send reminders and notifications to the patient and their caregiver (in my case, me) about upcoming appointments, appointment times, and any changes to the schedule. It would also be great if the system could allow us to easily schedule follow-up appointments or tests, like lab work, in the same platform, so we don't have to go back and forth between different websites or offices. And maybe even have the option to schedule appointments during off-peak hours or on weekends, when traffic and parking might be less of an issue.

I check their website or online directories like Healthgrades to see their availability and reviews.
